children.title: Validated Numerical Certification
children.top_down_role: Numerically computed certificates strengthened through rigorous validation.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is defined by polynomial inequalities \(g_i(x)\ge0\).
Outward-rounded interval arithmetic encloses every coefficient, matrix operation, and residual used by the verifier.
The verified interval Gram matrices have certified nonnegative lower spectral bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)\ge\underline{\gamma}\) for all \(x\in K\).

notation.meaning: Rigorous lower endpoint of the candidate bound.
Interval enclosure of the polynomial-identity residual.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interval validation of an approximate SOS lower-bound certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given approximate Gram matrices, a validated certificate consists of interval matrices \([Q_i]\), an interval residual polynomial \([r]\), and a bound \(\underline{\gamma}\) such that outward-rounded computation verifies \[f-\underline{\gamma}=v_0^{\mathsf T}[Q_0]v_0+\sum_{i=1}^m g_i v_i^{\mathsf T}[Q_i]v_i+[r].\] The verifier must certify \(Q_i\succeq0\) for every point matrix \(Q_i\in[Q_i]\) and certify that the residual contribution is nonnegative on \(K\), either directly or through an explicitly validated absorption into the SOS terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outward-rounded interval computations certify that all admissible Gram matrices are positive semidefinite and that the enclosed residual cannot invalidate the lower bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Validated Numerical Certification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role fits the container, but no source supports the proposed interval verifier or its residual-absorption conditions. The displayed equality involving interval-valued expressions also needs a precise enclosure or quantified interpretation, and the monomial vectors are not introduced. These details materially affect validity.

children.title: Speed-Certifiability Frontier
children.top_down_role: Tradeoff regimes connecting computational speed, bound quality, plus certification rigor.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{M}\) is a specified family of lower-bound methods for one polynomial optimization instance.
Each \(M\in\mathcal{M}\) has runtime \(T(M)\), certified bound \(L(M)\), and certification level \(C(M)\) in a fixed ordered scale.
Larger \(L\) and \(C\), but smaller \(T\), are preferred.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{F}=\{M\in\mathcal{M}:\nexists M'\in\mathcal{M}\text{ with }T(M')\le T(M),\ L(M')\ge L(M),\ C(M')\ge C(M)\text{ and one strict inequality}\}\).

notation.meaning: Returned lower bound, with larger values stronger.
Ordered rigor level of the accompanying certificate.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto frontier over runtime, lower-bound strength, and certificate rigor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A method \(M\in\mathcal{M}\) lies on the speed-certifiability frontier when no \(M'\in\mathcal{M}\) satisfies \[T(M')\le T(M),\qquad L(M')\ge L(M),\qquad C(M')\ge C(M),\] with at least one strict inequality. Thus frontier membership is relative to the fixed instance, implementation, resource limit, accuracy convention, and ordered certification scale; changing any of these data may change the nondominated set \(\mathcal{F}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The frontier contains methods not simultaneously beaten in runtime, bound strength, and certificate rigor under fixed computational and accuracy conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Speed-Certifiability Frontier

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent, the quantifiers are explicit, and definition is the appropriate content kind for this frontier container. A domain-specific source is still required for treating the selected runtime, bound-strength, and certification-level ordering as an established polynomial-optimization concept rather than a local formalization.

children.title: Rounding-Induced Certification Failures
children.top_down_role: Loss of validity or exact recoverability caused by finite-precision output.

assumptions_latex: \(Q\succeq0\) and \(p=v^{\mathsf T}Qv\) is a valid SOS representation.
A floating-point rounding procedure produces \(\widehat Q=Q+E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\lambda_{\min}(Q)=0\), arbitrarily small rounding may yield \(\widehat Q\not\succeq0\); independently, coefficient residuals may make \(v^{\mathsf T}\widehat Qv\ne p\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of PSD or polynomial identity under unvalidated rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rounded SOS certificate fails whenever either \(\widehat Q\not\succeq0\) or the exact coefficient identity \(p=v^{\mathsf T}\widehat Qv\) is false. Weyl's bound gives \[\lambda_{\min}(\widehat Q)\ge\lambda_{\min}(Q)-\lVert E\rVert_2,\] so positive semidefiniteness is protected only when a verified margin exceeds \(\lVert E\rVert_2\). If \(Q\) is singular, for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists symmetric \(E\) with \(\lVert E\rVert_2<\varepsilon\) such that \(Q+E\) has a negative eigenvalue. Even PSD-preserving rounding can leave a nonzero coefficient residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rounding can destroy Gram-matrix positivity or exact coefficient matching; singular certificates have no perturbation margin protecting positive semidefiniteness.
knowledge_statements.title: Rounding-Induced Certification Failures

children.title: Scalability Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural patterns that defeat nominal sparsity or undermine computational reliability.

children.title: Dense Chordal Completion
children.top_down_role: Sparse input patterns whose completions create large cliques.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is the correlative-sparsity graph and \(H\supseteq G\) is a chordal completion.
\(C_1,\ldots,C_q\) are the maximal cliques of \(H\), and relaxation order \(d\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A clique block indexed by monomials of degree at most \(d\) in \(C_k\) has dimension \(\binom{|C_k|+d}{d}\); hence a large completion clique destroys sparse block savings.

notation.meaning: Chordal completion of the sparsity graph.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clique-size failure mechanism in chordal sparse moment-SOS relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For relaxation order \(d\), the local moment or Gram block associated with a maximal clique \(C_k\) contains all monomials in \(|C_k|\) variables of degree at most \(d\), so its dimension is \[s_k=\binom{|C_k|+d}{d}.\] If every chordal completion permitted by the chosen elimination constraints has \(\max_k|C_k|\ge w+1\), then the relaxation contains a positive-semidefinite block of dimension at least \(\binom{w+1+d}{d}\). Thus sparse input alone does not ensure small semidefinite blocks: completion fill can create a nearly dense clique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Chordal fill can turn a sparse interaction graph into large cliques, producing moment or Gram blocks whose dimension grows combinatorially with clique size.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense Chordal Completion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits Dense Chordal Completion, but the claim depends on the precise sparse moment-SOS construction and chordal-completion restrictions. No source is supplied for the block indexing or the asserted unavoidable-clique lower bound, so the mathematical scope cannot yet be validated.

children.title: Large-Separator Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Strong coupling caused by large clique intersections.

assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_q\) form a clique tree for a chordal sparse relaxation.
Each adjacent pair \((i,j)\) has separator \(S_{ij}=C_i\cap C_j\), and moments through degree \(2d\) must agree on overlaps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each separator requires \(\binom{|S_{ij}|+2d}{2d}\) shared moment coordinates or consistency equalities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Overlap-consistency cost in clique-tree moment relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an edge \((i,j)\) of the clique tree, consistency of the local truncated moment sequences requires \[y^{(i)}_\alpha=y^{(j)}_\alpha\qquad\text{for every }\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{S_{ij}}\text{ with }|\alpha|\le2d.\] The number of indexed overlap moments is exactly \(\binom{|S_{ij}|+2d}{2d}\). Consequently, a separator of size \(s\) creates that many coupling coordinates or equality constraints, and large separators can dominate communication, assembly, and factorization costs even when individual cliques remain moderate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separator of size s couples local relaxations through binomially many shared moments, so large clique intersections can dominate computational cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Large-Separator Bottlenecks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Complexity bound is an appropriate content kind for the separator bottleneck. The monomial count is combinatorially plausible, but whether it gives shared coordinates, explicit equality constraints, or a reduced parametrization depends on the sparse relaxation formulation. A sparse-moment consistency source is required.

children.title: Support-Fill Explosion
children.top_down_role: Rapid growth of term graphs under support extension.

assumptions_latex: \(A_0\subseteq\mathbb{N}^n\) is a finite monomial support with \(0\in A_0\).
Support extension is defined recursively by \(A_{t+1}=A_t\cup(A_t+A_t)\), where \(A+B=\{\alpha+\beta:\alpha\in A,\beta\in B\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_t\subseteq 2^t\operatorname{conv}(A_0)\cap\mathbb{N}^n\), while \(|A_{t+1}|\le |A_t|+|A_t|^2\).

notation.meaning: Convex hull of the initial support.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial support growth under a representative Minkowski-extension rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated extension rule and the assumption \(0\in A_0\), every exponent in \(A_t\) lies in \(2^t\operatorname{conv}(A_0)\), and \[|A_{t+1}|\le |A_t|+|A_t|^2.\] Before repeated sums collide, the number of candidate exponents can grow quadratically in one extension and rapidly across iterations. A term graph placing edges between monomials whose sums enter \(A_{t+1}\) may simultaneously acquire dense components, so support-based block structure can disappear even though \(A_0\) is small.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a support containing the constant exponent, repeated Minkowski extension can generate quadratically many candidate exponents per round and may densify term graphs, erasing initial term sparsity.
knowledge_statements.title: Support-Fill Explosion

children.title: High-Degree Local Blocks
children.top_down_role: Large local moment blocks despite favorable global sparsity.

assumptions_latex: A local clique or variable block contains \(r\) variables.
The local moment-SOS relaxation has order \(d\), so moments through degree \(2d\) are retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The moment matrix has dimension \(\binom{r+d}{d}\), and the local truncated moment vector contains \(\binom{r+2d}{2d}\) entries.

notation.meaning: Number of variables in the local block.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial local-block growth with relaxation degree.

source_refs.locator: 5.3 Constrained Polynomial Optimization: Semidefinite Relaxations p. 117
source_refs.source_title: Moments, Positive Polynomials and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The monomial vector of degree at most \(d\) in \(r\) variables has length \[s(r,d)=\binom{r+d}{d}.\] Hence its local moment matrix is an \(s(r,d)\times s(r,d)\) positive-semidefinite block, while the truncated local moment sequence through degree \(2d\) has \(\binom{r+2d}{2d}\) coordinates. For fixed favorable global sparsity, increasing \(d\) can therefore make a single local block computationally dominant; global sparsity does not control this degree-driven growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even with strong global sparsity, a local block grows combinatorially with relaxation degree and can dominate the semidefinite relaxation.
knowledge_statements.title: High-Degree Local Blocks

source_witnesses.locator: 5.3 Constrained Polynomial Optimization: Semidefinite Relaxations p. 117
source_witnesses.source_title: Moments, Positive Polynomials and Their Applications

children.title: Numerically Fragile Sparse Models
children.top_down_role: Sparse formulations impaired by scaling, overlap, or degeneracy.

assumptions_latex: A sparse moment-SOS model contains local positive-semidefinite blocks \(Q_k\) and linear overlap constraints \(Aq=b\).
Data scaling or degeneracy makes either a block nearly singular or the constraint operator nearly rank deficient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\min_k\lambda_{\min}^{+}(Q_k)\) or \(\sigma_{\min}^{+}(A)\) is small relative to perturbations, computed feasibility need not imply a stable recoverable certificate.

notation.meaning: Linear consistency operator and stacked coefficients.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditioning failure from scaling, overlap dependencies, or degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let perturbations in the assembled sparse relaxation have norm at most \(\varepsilon\). If a positive-semidefinite block has spectral margin comparable to \(\varepsilon\), its numerical rank and cone membership are unstable. If \(\sigma_{\min}^{+}(A)\) is comparable to \(\varepsilon\), overlap corrections solving \(A\Delta q=-r\) may satisfy \(\lVert\Delta q\rVert_2\) of order \(\lVert r\rVert_2/\sigma_{\min}^{+}(A)\). Thus poor scaling, redundant overlap equations, or facial degeneracy can prevent stable certificate recovery despite small solver residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nearly singular blocks or overlap systems amplify numerical errors, so a sparse model may be computationally small yet unsuitable for stable certificate recovery.
knowledge_statements.title: Numerically Fragile Sparse Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind matches the numerical-fragility container. However, no source supports the perturbation thresholds or their application to sparse SDP certificate recovery. The overlap-correction estimate also depends on solvability or projection of the residual onto the range of the constraint operator, which is not stated.

children.title: Solver-Accuracy Certification Gap
children.top_down_role: Mismatch between scalable solver tolerances and certificate-recovery requirements.

assumptions_latex: A solver returns approximate primal-dual variables with residual tolerance \(\tau>0\).
Certificate recovery requires exact coefficient equalities and positive-semidefinite Gram matrices after correction.
The candidate Gram matrix has spectral margin \(\delta\), and recovery changes it by \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Recovery is guaranteed by these tests only if exact residual correction succeeds and \(\lVert E\rVert_2<\delta\); a solver report with residual at most \(\tau\) alone is insufficient.

notation.meaning: Exact-recovery perturbation of a Gram matrix.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between approximate SDP feasibility and rigorous certificate recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A termination report asserting residuals at most \(\tau\) establishes only approximate feasibility under the solver's norms and scaling. A rigorous polynomial certificate additionally requires exact coefficient identities and exact or validated cone membership. If \(Q\succeq\delta I\) and recovery replaces \(Q\) by \(Q+E\), then \(\lVert E\rVert_2<\delta\) preserves positive definiteness. When no verified margin exists, or exact residual correction requires a perturbation at least \(\delta\), an arbitrarily small reported solver residual does not by itself yield a certifiable bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small solver residuals certify only approximate feasibility; rigorous recovery also needs exact identities and enough spectral margin to survive correction.
knowledge_statements.title: Solver-Accuracy Certification Gap

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the solver-accuracy certification gap, and the distinction between approximate solver feasibility and rigorous recovery is mathematically coherent. A source is required for the recovery conditions, while the meaning of the reported tolerance must be tied to a specified solver's norms, scaling, and stopping tests.
